claim: The Aquilegia genus is made up of about 70 species distributed across Asia, North America, and Europe.
source: The genus is made up of about 70 species distributed across Asia, North America, and Europe (Munz, 1946) (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by citation to Munz, 1946 and reference to Figure 1 showing geographic distribution.

claim: Distributions of many Aquilegia species overlap or adjoin one another, sometimes forming notable hybrid zones.
source: Distributions of many Aquilegia species overlap or adjoin one another, sometimes forming notable hybrid zones (Grant, 1952; Hodges and Arnold, 1994b; Li et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Grant, 1952; Hodges and Arnold, 1994b; Li et al., 2014.

claim: Aquilegia species tend to be widely interfertile, especially within geographic regions.
source: Additionally, species tend to be widely interfertile, especially within geographic regions (Taylor, 1967).
evidence: Supported by citation to Taylor, 1967.

claim: Phylogenetic studies have defined two concurrent, yet contrasting, adaptive radiations in Aquilegia.
source: Phylogenetic studies have defined two concurrent, yet contrasting, adaptive radiations in Aquilegia (Bastida et al., 2010; Fior et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bastida et al., 2010; Fior et al., 2013.

claim: From a common ancestor in Asia, one radiation occurred in North America via Northeastern Asian precursors, while a separate Eurasian radiation took place in central and western Asia and Europe.
source: From a common ancestor in Asia, one radiation occurred in North America via Northeastern Asian precursors, while a separate Eurasian radiation took place in central and western Asia and Europe.
evidence: This is a statement about phylogenetic relationships based on previous studies mentioned in the context.

claim: Adaptation to different habitats is thought to be a common force driving both Aquilegia radiations.
source: While adaptation to different habitats is thought to be a common force driving both radiations, shifts in primary pollinators also play a substantial role in North America (Whittall and Hodges, 2007; Bastida et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Whittall and Hodges, 2007; Bastida et al., 2010.

claim: Shifts in primary pollinators play a substantial role in the North American Aquilegia radiation.
source: While adaptation to different habitats is thought to be a common force driving both radiations, shifts in primary pollinators also play a substantial role in North America (Whittall and Hodges, 2007; Bastida et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Whittall and Hodges, 2007; Bastida et al., 2010.

claim: Previous phylogenetic studies have frequently revealed polytomies in Aquilegia, suggesting that many species are very closely related.
source: Previous phylogenetic studies have frequently revealed polytomies (Hodges and Arnold, 1994b; Ro et al., 1997; Whittall and Hodges, 2007; Bastida et al., 2010; Fior et al., 2013), suggesting that many Aquilegia species are very closely related.
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple phylogenetic studies and inference about species relationships.

claim: The A. coerulea 'Goldsmith' genome assembly consists of 2529 scaffolds with an N50 of 3.1 Mbp.
source: A total of 4,773,210 Sanger sequencing reads from seven genomic libraries (Supplementary file 1) were assembled to generate 2529 scaffolds with an N50 of 3.1 Mbp (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data from genome sequencing and assembly.

claim: The A. coerulea 'Goldsmith' reference genome is 291.7 Mbp consisting of 7 chromosomes (282.6 Mbp) and 1027 unplaced scaffolds (9.13 Mbp).
source: With the aid of two genetic maps, we assembled these initial scaffolds into a 291.7 Mbp reference genome consisting of 7 chromosomes (282.6 Mbp) and an additional 1027 unplaced scaffolds (9.13 Mbp) (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data from genome assembly.

claim: 98.69% of 81,617 full length cDNAs mapped to the A. coerulea 'Goldsmith' assembly.
source: The completeness of the assembly was validated using 81,617 full length cDNAs from a variety of tissues and developmental stages (Kramer and Hodges, 2010), of which 98.69% mapped to the assembly.
evidence: This is experimental data validating genome assembly completeness.

claim: Only 1831 base pairs out of more than 3 million were found to be discrepant between BAC clones and the assembled reference.
source: We also assessed assembly accuracy using Sanger sequencing of 23 full-length BAC clones. Of more than 3 million base pairs sequenced, only 1831 were found to be discrepant between BAC clones and the assembled reference (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is experimental data validating genome assembly accuracy.

claim: The A. coerulea 'Goldsmith' genome annotation yielded 30,023 loci and 13,527 alternate transcripts.
source: To annotate genes in the assembly, we used RNAseq data generated from a variety of tissues and Aquilegia species (Supplementary file 5), EST data sets (Kramer and Hodges, 2010), and protein homology support, yielding 30,023 loci and 13,527 alternate transcripts.
evidence: This is a direct report of genome annotation results.

claim: Most of the ten sequenced Aquilegia individuals had a nucleotide diversity of 0.2–0.35%.
source: Of the ten individuals, most had a nucleotide diversity of 0.2–0.35% (Figure 2a), similar to previous estimates of nucleotide diversity in Aquilegia (Cooper et al., 2010), yet lower than that of a typical outcrossing species (Leffler et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2a and citations to Cooper et al., 2010 and Leffler et al., 2012.

claim: Nucleotide diversity in Aquilegia is lower than that of a typical outcrossing species.
source: Of the ten individuals, most had a nucleotide diversity of 0.2–0.35% (Figure 2a), similar to previous estimates of nucleotide diversity in Aquilegia (Cooper et al., 2010), yet lower than that of a typical outcrossing species (Leffler et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by comparison to data from Leffler et al., 2012.

claim: Four individuals in the Aquilegia panel had extended stretches of near-homozygosity consistent with recent inbreeding.
source: Additionally, four individuals in our panel had extended stretches of near-homozygosity (defined as nucleotide diversity <0.1%) consistent with recent inbreeding (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Aquilegia has no known self-incompatibility mechanism.
source: Aquilegia has no known self-incompatibility mechanism, and selfing does appear to be common.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about Aquilegia reproductive biology.

claim: Inbreeding in adult Aquilegia plants is generally low, suggesting substantial inbreeding depression.
source: However, inbreeding in adult plants is generally low, suggesting substantial inbreeding depression (Montalvo, 1994; Herlihy and Eckert, 2002; Yang and Hodges, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Montalvo, 1994; Herlihy and Eckert, 2002; Yang and Hodges, 2010.

claim: Species divergence within a geographic region (0.38–0.86%) was often only slightly higher than within-species diversity in Aquilegia.
source: Species divergence within a geographic region (0.38–0.86%) was often only slightly higher than within-species diversity, implying extensive variant sharing, while divergence between species from different geographic regions was markedly higher (0.81–0.97%; Figure 2a).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Divergence between Aquilegia species from different geographic regions was markedly higher (0.81–0.97%).
source: Species divergence within a geographic region (0.38–0.86%) was often only slightly higher than within-species diversity, implying extensive variant sharing, while divergence between species from different geographic regions was markedly higher (0.81–0.97%; Figure 2a).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The topology of trees constructed with concatenated genome data were in broad agreement with previous Aquilegia phylogenies, with one exception regarding A. oxysepala placement.
source: The topology of trees constructed with concatenated genome data (neighbor joining (Figure 2a), RAxML (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a)) were in broad agreement with previous Aquilegia phylogenies (Hodges and Arnold, 1994a; Ro and McPheron, 1997; Whittall and Hodges, 2007; Bastida et al., 2010; Fior et al., 2013), with one exception: while A. oxysepala is sister to all other Aquilegia species in our analysis, it had been placed within the large Eurasian clade with moderate to strong support in previous studies (Bastida et al., 2010; Fior et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by comparison to multiple previous phylogenetic studies and data shown in figures.

claim: A. oxysepala is sister to all other Aquilegia species in the genome tree analysis.
source: The topology of trees constructed with concatenated genome data (neighbor joining (Figure 2a), RAxML (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a)) were in broad agreement with previous Aquilegia phylogenies (Hodges and Arnold, 1994a; Ro and McPheron, 1997; Whittall and Hodges, 2007; Bastida et al., 2010; Fior et al., 2013), with one exception: while A. oxysepala is sister to all other Aquilegia species in our analysis, it had been placed within the large Eurasian clade with moderate to strong support in previous studies (Bastida et al., 2010; Fior et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 2a.

claim: Levels of polymorphism were generally strikingly higher on chromosome four.
source: Surprisingly, levels of polymorphism were generally strikingly higher on chromosome four (Figure 2b).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The increased polymorphism on chromosome four is only partly reflected in increased divergence to an outgroup species (Semiaquilegia adoxoides).
source: The increased polymorphism on chromosome four is only partly reflected in increased divergence to an outgroup species (Semiaquilegia adoxoides), suggesting that it represents deeper coalescence times rather than simply a higher mutation rate (mean ratio chromosome four/genome at fourfold degenerate sites: polymorphism = 2.258, divergence = 1.201, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: Supported by data in Supplementary file 6 and inference about coalescence times.

claim: Fewer than 1% of window-based trees were topologically identical to the species tree.
source: Fewer than 1% of these window-based trees were topologically identical to the species tree.
evidence: This is a direct report of data from window-based tree analysis.

claim: North American species were consistently separated from all others in 96% of window trees.
source: North American species were consistently separated from all others (96% of window trees) and European species were also clearly delineated (67% of window trees).
evidence: This is a direct report of data from window-based tree analysis.

claim: European species were clearly delineated in 67% of window trees.
source: North American species were consistently separated from all others (96% of window trees) and European species were also clearly delineated (67% of window trees).
evidence: This is a direct report of data from window-based tree analysis.

claim: Three bifurcations delineating Asian species were much less common in window trees: the A. japonica and A. sibirica sister relationship (45%), A. oxysepala as sister to all other species (30%), and the split demarcating the Eurasian radiation (31%).
source: However, three bifurcations delineating Asian species were much less common: the A. japonica and A. sibirica sister relationship (45% of window trees), A. oxysepala as sister to all other species (30% of window trees), and the split demarcating the Eurasian radiation (31% of window trees).
evidence: This is a direct report of data from window-based tree analysis.

claim: There is marked discordance of gene and species trees throughout both Aquilegia radiations.
source: These results demonstrate a marked discordance of gene and species trees throughout both Aquilegia radiations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the window-based tree analysis data.

claim: Nine subtrees varied significantly in frequency between chromosomes.
source: Of 217 unique subtrees observed in gene trees, nine varied significantly in frequency between chromosomes (chi-square test p-value < 0.05 after Bonferroni correction; Figure 3b–d and Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and data shown in figures.

claim: Trees describing a sister species relationship between A. pubescens and A. barnebyi were more common on chromosome one.
source: Trees describing a sister species relationship between A. pubescens and A. barnebyi were more common on chromosome one, but chromosome four stood out with respect to eight other relationships, most of them related to A. oxysepala (Figure 3d).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Chromosome four stood out with respect to eight relationships, most of them related to A. oxysepala.
source: Trees describing a sister species relationship between A. pubescens and A. barnebyi were more common on chromosome one, but chromosome four stood out with respect to eight other relationships, most of them related to A. oxysepala (Figure 3d).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: The topology of the chromosome four tree placed A. oxysepala within the Eurasian clade, consistent with previously-published phylogenies.
source: Although A. oxysepala was sister to all other species in our genome tree, the topology of the chromosome four tree was consistent with previously-published phylogenies in that it placed A. oxysepala within the Eurasian clade (Bastida et al., 2010; Fior et al., 2013) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2b,c).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2b,c and citations to Bastida et al., 2010; Fior et al., 2013.

claim: No patterns in the prevalence of any chromosome-discordant subtree suggested structural variation or a large introgression.
source: We detected no patterns in the prevalence of any chromosome-discordant subtree that would suggest structural variation or a large introgression (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Private derived variants accounted for only 21–25% of polymorphic sites in North American species.
source: Private derived variants accounted for only 21–25% of polymorphic sites in North American species and 36–47% of variants in Eurasian species (Figure 4a).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Private derived variants accounted for 36–47% of variants in Eurasian species.
source: Private derived variants accounted for only 21–25% of polymorphic sites in North American species and 36–47% of variants in Eurasian species (Figure 4a).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: North American species shared 34–38% of their derived variants within North America.
source: North American species shared 34–38% of their derived variants within North America, while variants in European and Asian species were commonly shared across two geographic regions (18–22% of polymorphisms, predominantly shared between Europe and Asia; Figure 4b,c; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4b,c and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Variants in European and Asian species were commonly shared across two geographic regions (18–22% of polymorphisms, predominantly shared between Europe and Asia).
source: North American species shared 34–38% of their derived variants within North America, while variants in European and Asian species were commonly shared across two geographic regions (18–22% of polymorphisms, predominantly shared between Europe and Asia; Figure 4b,c; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4b,c and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: A large percentage of derived variants occurred in all three geographic regions (22–32% of polymorphisms).
source: Strikingly, a large percentage of derived variants occurred in all three geographic regions (22–32% of polymorphisms, Figure 4d), demonstrating that polymorphism sharing in Aquilegia is extensive and deep.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Polymorphism sharing in Aquilegia is extensive and deep.
source: Strikingly, a large percentage of derived variants occurred in all three geographic regions (22–32% of polymorphisms, Figure 4d), demonstrating that polymorphism sharing in Aquilegia is extensive and deep.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data about variant sharing across geographic regions.

claim: The proportion of deeply shared variants was higher on chromosome four in all species examined.
source: In all species examined, the proportion of deeply shared variants was higher on chromosome four (Figure 4d), largely due to a reduction in private variants, although sharing at other depths was also reduced in some species.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Variant sharing on chromosome four within Asia was higher in both A. oxysepala and A. japonica.
source: Variant sharing on chromosome four within Asia was higher in both A. oxysepala and A. japonica (Figure 4b), primarily reflecting higher variant sharing between these species (Figure 6a).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4b and Figure 6a.

claim: The North American split was closest to resembling speciation with strict reproductive isolation, with little asymmetry in allele sharing between North American and Asian species.
source: As predicted, the North American split was closest to resembling speciation with strict reproductive isolation, with little asymmetry in allele sharing between North American and Asian species and low, but significant, asymmetry between North American and European species (Figure 5b).
evidence: Supported by D statistic analysis shown in Figure 5b.

claim: There was low, but significant, asymmetry in allele sharing between North American and European species.
source: As predicted, the North American split was closest to resembling speciation with strict reproductive isolation, with little asymmetry in allele sharing between North American and Asian species and low, but significant, asymmetry between North American and European species (Figure 5b).
evidence: Supported by D statistic analysis shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Non-zero D statistics were found for all species combinations between European and Asian species.
source: Next, we considered allele sharing between European and Asian (without A. oxysepala) species (Figure 5d,e). Here we found non-zero D statistics for all species combinations.
evidence: Supported by D statistic analysis shown in Figure 5d,e.

claim: Asian species shared more variants with the European A. vulgaris while European species shared more derived alleles with the Asian A. sibirica.
source: Interestingly, the patterns of asymmetry between these two regions were reticulate: Asian species shared more variants with the European A. vulgaris while European species shared more derived alleles with the Asian A. sibirica.
evidence: This is an inference based on D statistic analysis.

claim: D statistics demonstrate widespread asymmetry in variant sharing between Aquilegia species, suggesting that speciation processes throughout the genus were not characterized by strict reproductive isolation.
source: D statistics therefore demonstrate widespread asymmetry in variant sharing between Aquilegia species, suggesting that speciation processes throughout the genus were not characterized by strict reproductive isolation.
evidence: This is an inference based on D statistic analysis.

claim: D statistics do not differ when calculated with only fourfold degenerate sites (p-value < 2.2 x 10-16, adjusted R2 = 0.9942).
source: The possibility that different levels of purifying selection in H1 or H2 explain the observed D statistics can probably be ruled out, since D statistics do not differ when calculated with only fourfold degenerate sites (p-value < 2.2 x 10-16, adjusted R2 = 0.9942, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis reported in Figure 5—source data 1.

claim: The non-zero D statistics observed in Aquilegia most likely reflect a pattern of reticulate evolution throughout the genus.
source: Therefore, the non-zero D statistics observed in Aquilegia most likely reflect a pattern of reticulate evolution throughout the genus.
evidence: This is an inference based on D statistic analysis and ruling out alternative explanations.

claim: Hybridization between A. oxysepala and A. japonica has been reported.
source: Since variant sharing between A. oxysepala and A. japonica was higher on chromosome four (Figure 6a), and hybridization between these species has been reported (Li et al., 2014) we wondered whether gene flow could explain the discordant placement of A. oxysepala between chromosome four and genome trees (Figure 3b,c).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2014.

claim: Doubling the population size (N) to reflect chromosome four's polymorphism level could shift tree topology proportions.
source: A relatively simple coalescent model allowing for bidirectional gene flow between A. oxysepala and A. japonica (Figure 6b) demonstrated that doubling the population size (N) to reflect chromosome four's polymorphism level (i.e. halving the coalescence rate) could indeed shift tree topology proportions (Figure 6c, row 2).
evidence: Supported by coalescent modeling results shown in Figure 6b,c.

claim: Recreating the observed allele sharing ratios on chromosome four required some combination of increased migration (m) and/or N.
source: However, recreating the observed allele sharing ratios on chromosome four (Figure 6a) required some combination of increased migration (m) and/or N (Figure 6c, rows 3–4).
evidence: Supported by coalescent modeling results shown in Figure 6a,c.

claim: An increase in migration rate and deeper coalescence can explain the tree topology of chromosome four.
source: Therefore, an increase in migration rate and deeper coalescence can explain the tree topology of chromosome four, a result that might explain inconsistencies in A. oxysepala placement in previous phylogenetic studies (Bastida et al., 2010; Fior et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on coalescent modeling results and comparison to previous studies.

claim: The level of polymorphism on chromosome four is twice as high as in the rest of the genome in most of the sequenced Aquilegia species.
source: In most of the sequenced Aquilegia species, the level of polymorphism on chromosome four is twice as high as in the rest of the genome (Figure 2b).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The pattern of elevated polymorphism on chromosome four cannot wholly be explained by a higher neutral mutation rate.
source: Similarly, the pattern cannot wholly be explained by a higher neutral mutation rate. If this were the case, both divergence and polymorphism would be elevated to the same extent on chromosome four (Kimura, 1983). As noted above, this not the case (Supplementary file 6).
evidence: Supported by comparison of polymorphism and divergence data in Supplementary file 6 and citation to Kimura, 1983.

claim: The higher level of polymorphism on chromosome four must to some extent reflect differences in coalescence time, which can only be due to selection.
source: Thus the higher level of polymorphism on chromosome four must to some extent reflect differences in coalescence time, which can only be due to selection.
evidence: This is an inference based on ruling out alternative explanations.

claim: Chromosome four recombines freely.
source: Chromosome four recombines freely (Figure 7a), suggesting that polymorphism is not due to selection on a limited number of linked loci, such as might be observed if driven by an inversion or large supergene.
evidence: Supported by recombination data shown in Figure 7a.

claim: Selection must be acting on a very large number of loci across chromosome four.
source: Selection must thus be acting on a very large number of loci across the chromosome.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that chromosome four recombines freely yet has elevated polymorphism.

claim: Chromosome four is enriched for the defense gene GO category, which encompasses R genes.
source: While such signatures have not yet been demonstrated in Aquilegia, chromosome four is enriched for the defense gene GO category, which encompasses R genes (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by GO term enrichment analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: Defense gene enrichment on chromosome four involves a relatively small number of genes (less than 2% of genes on chromosome four) and is unlikely to completely explain the polymorphism pattern.
source: However, while significant, this enrichment involves a relatively small number of genes (less than 2% of genes on chromosome four) and is therefore unlikely to completely explain the polymorphism pattern (Nordborg and Innan, 2003).
evidence: This is an inference based on the proportion of defense genes and citation to Nordborg and Innan, 2003.

claim: Gene density is markedly lower on chromosome four.
source: Gene density is markedly lower (Table 2 and Figure 7b), it harbors a higher proportion of repetitive sites (Table 2), and is enriched for many transposon families, including Copia and Gypsy elements (Supplementary file 8).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Table 2 and Figure 7b.

claim: Chromosome four harbors a higher proportion of repetitive sites.
source: Gene density is markedly lower (Table 2 and Figure 7b), it harbors a higher proportion of repetitive sites (Table 2), and is enriched for many transposon families, including Copia and Gypsy elements (Supplementary file 8).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Table 2.

claim: Chromosome four is enriched for many transposon families, including Copia and Gypsy elements.
source: Gene density is markedly lower (Table 2 and Figure 7b), it harbors a higher proportion of repetitive sites (Table 2), and is enriched for many transposon families, including Copia and Gypsy elements (Supplementary file 8).
evidence: Supported by data in Supplementary file 8.

claim: A higher proportion of genes on chromosome four were either not expressed or expressed at a low level.
source: Additionally, a higher proportion of genes on chromosome four were either not expressed or expressed at a low level (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Gene models on chromosome four were more likely to contain variants that could disrupt protein function.
source: Gene models on the chromosome were also more likely to contain variants that could disrupt protein function (Table 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Table 2.

claim: These observations suggest less purifying selection on chromosome four.
source: Taken together, these observations suggest less purifying selection on chromosome four.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple lines of evidence about chromosome four characteristics.

claim: There is a negative relationship between introgression and gene density in the Aquilegia genome.
source: Indeed, focusing on A. oxysepala/A. japonica gene flow, we found a negative relationship between introgression and gene density in the Aquilegia genome (Figure 7c, p-value = 2.202 x 10-7, adjusted R-squared = 0.068), as would be expected if purifying selection limited introgression.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and data shown in Figure 7c.

claim: There is a negative relationship between gene density and neutral nucleotide diversity genome-wide.
source: While there is a negative relationship between gene density and neutral nucleotide diversity genome-wide (p-value = 5.174 x 10-6, adjusted R2 = 0.052), more careful analysis reveals that chromosome four has a completely different distribution from the rest of the genome (Figure 7d, p-value < 2 x 10-16).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and data shown in Figure 7d.

claim: Chromosome four has a completely different distribution of nucleotide diversity versus gene density from the rest of the genome.
source: While there is a negative relationship between gene density and neutral nucleotide diversity genome-wide (p-value = 5.174 x 10-6, adjusted R2 = 0.052), more careful analysis reveals that chromosome four has a completely different distribution from the rest of the genome (Figure 7d, p-value < 2 x 10-16).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and data shown in Figure 7d.

claim: Gene density differences alone are insufficient to explain higher polymorphism on chromosome four.
source: Thus the genome-wide relationship reflects this systematic difference between chromosome four and the rest of the genome, and gene density differences alone are insufficient to explain higher polymorphism on chromosome four.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of gene density and nucleotide diversity relationships.

claim: There is a significant relationship between neutral diversity and recombination rate in Aquilegia (without chromosome four, Kendall's tau = 0.222, p-value = 3.804 x 10-6).
source: For comparison with data from other organisms, we performed the partial correlation analysis of Corbett-Detig et al. (2015). Here we found a significant relationship between neutral diversity and recombination rate (without chromosome four, Kendall's tau = 0.222, p-value = 3.804 x 10-6), putting Aquilegia on the higher end of estimates of the strength of linked selection in herbaceous plants.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis following the method of Corbett-Detig et al. (2015).

claim: The pattern of polymorphism on chromosome four predates the Aquilegia radiation.
source: While selection during the Aquilegia radiation contributes to the pattern of polymorphism on chromosome four, the pattern itself predates the radiation.
evidence: This is an inference based on divergence and polymorphism data in Semiaquilegia.

claim: Divergence between Aquilegia and Semiaquilegia is higher on chromosome four (2.77% on chromosome four, 2.48% genome-wide).
source: Divergence between Aquilegia and Semiaquilegia is higher on chromosome four (2.77% on chromosome four, 2.48% genome-wide, Table 3), as is nucleotide diversity within Semiaquilegia (0.16% chromosome four, 0.08% genome-wide, Table 3).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Table 3.

claim: Nucleotide diversity within Semiaquilegia is higher on chromosome four (0.16% chromosome four, 0.08% genome-wide).
source: Divergence between Aquilegia and Semiaquilegia is higher on chromosome four (2.77% on chromosome four, 2.48% genome-wide, Table 3), as is nucleotide diversity within Semiaquilegia (0.16% chromosome four, 0.08% genome-wide, Table 3).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Table 3.

claim: The variant evolutionary history of chromosome four began before the Aquilegia/Semiaquilegia split.
source: This suggests that the variant evolutionary history of chromosome four began before the Aquilegia/Semiaquilegia split.
evidence: This is an inference based on divergence and polymorphism data in Semiaquilegia.

claim: Both the 35S and 5S rDNA loci were localized uniquely to chromosome four in two Aquilegia species and S. adoxoides.
source: Using fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) with rDNA and chromosome four-specific bulked oligo probes (Han et al., 2015), we confirmed that both the 35S and 5S rDNA loci were localized uniquely to chromosome four in two Aquilegia species and S. adoxoides (Figure 8).
evidence: Supported by FISH data shown in Figure 8 and citation to Han et al., 2015.

claim: Chromosome four contained a single large 35S repeat cluster proximal to the centromeric region in all three species examined.
source: The chromosome contained a single large 35S repeat cluster proximal to the centromeric region in all three species.
evidence: This is a direct observation from FISH analysis.

claim: The 35S locus in A. formosa was larger than that of the other two species and formed variable bubbles and fold-backs on extended pachytene chromosomes.
source: Interestingly, the 35S locus in A. formosa was larger than that of the other two species and formed variable bubbles and fold-backs on extended pachytene chromosomes similar to structures previously observed in Aquilegia hybrids (Linnert, 1961) (Figure 8, last panels).
evidence: Supported by FISH data shown in Figure 8 and citation to Linnert, 1961.

claim: The 5S rDNA locus was proximal to the centromere on chromosome four.
source: The 5S rDNA locus was also proximal to the centromere on chromosome four, although slight differences in the number and position of the 5S repeats between species highlight the dynamic nature of this gene cluster.
evidence: This is a direct observation from FISH analysis.

claim: No chromosome appeared to be more heterochromatic than others in the FISH analyses.
source: However, no chromosome appeared to be more heterochromatic than others in our analyses (Figure 8); FISH with 5-methylcytosine antibody showed no evidence for hypermethylation on chromosome four (Figure 8—figure supplement 1) and GC content was similar for all chromosomes (Table 2).
evidence: Supported by FISH data shown in Figure 8 and Figure 8—figure supplement 1, and data in Table 2.

claim: Similarities in chromosome four organization across all three species reinforce the idea that the exceptionality of this chromosome predated the Aquilegia/Semiaquilegia split.
source: However, similarities in chromosome four organization across all three species reinforce the idea that the exceptionality of this chromosome predated the Aquilegia/Semiaquilegia split and raise the possibility that rDNA clusters could have played a role in the variant evolutionary history of chromosome four.
evidence: This is an inference based on FISH observations across species.

claim: Variant sharing across the Aquilegia genus is widespread and deep, even across exceptionally large geographical distances.
source: Variant sharing across the Aquilegia genus is widespread and deep, even across exceptionally large geographical distances.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the variant sharing analysis.

claim: Asymmetry of allele sharing demonstrates that the process of speciation has been reticulate throughout the genus, and that gene flow has been a common feature.
source: Although much of this sharing is presumably due to stochastic processes, as expected given the rapid time-scale of speciation, asymmetry of allele sharing demonstrates that the process of speciation has been reticulate throughout the genus, and that gene flow has been a common feature.
evidence: This is an inference based on D statistic analysis.

claim: Aquilegia species diversity appears to be an example of ecological speciation, rather than being driven by the development of intrinsic barriers to gene flow.
source: Aquilegia species diversity therefore appears to be an example of ecological speciation, rather than being driven by the development of intrinsic barriers to gene flow (Coyne et al., 2004; Schluter and Conte, 2009; Seehausen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the evidence of gene flow and citations to Coyne et al., 2004; Schluter and Conte, 2009; Seehausen et al., 2014.

claim: The average level of polymorphism on chromosome four is roughly twice that of the rest of the genome.
